canonical_topic: Midcontinent (MISO) power market geography and fundamentals
definition: MISO (formerly the Midwest ISO) coordinates power across much of the central United States, with Indiana Hub (formerly Cin-Hub) as its most influential trading location.
core_idea: Coal-fired plants, including many marginal producers in the industrialized north, keep coal prices the primary driver of Midwest power prices even during high-demand periods, while the more rural south depends heavily on natural gas.
key_points: The northeastern part of MISO is heavily industrialized; the southern and northwestern sections are more rural.
Indiana Hub (previously Cin-Hub) is described as the most influential trading location in the region.

The region has cold winters (often starting as early as November, typically lasting through April) and hot, humid summers (July-August) that cool quickly by September; the southern part of MISO has milder winters and hot summers.
Coal powers many northern plants, including marginal producers, so coal prices commonly set Midwest power prices even in high-demand periods.
The southern MISO territory relies heavily on natural gas.
Because the Midwest's shoulder seasons (spring/fall) are cool, power is often wheeled south to hotter states during those periods.
Some hydroelectric power is available from the Great Lakes and Tennessee Valley areas and may be imported depending on the time of year.
relationships: Coal-driven marginal pricing parallels western PJM; south-to-north gas dependence contrasts with MISO's north.
trading_implications: Coal price moves are a stronger driver of Midwest power prices than in gas-dominated regions, even at peak demand.
Seasonal wheeling of power from the cooler Midwest to hotter southern states creates predictable seasonal flow/basis patterns.
Hydro availability from the Great Lakes/Tennessee Valley is a seasonal import option affecting regional supply.
caveats: Assuming natural gas dominates Midwest power pricing the way it does in many other US markets; in MISO's north, coal remains the marginal fuel even at peak demand.
